answer.rationale: Timing is the strongest available signal: latency onset (90 min ago) sits inside the window opened by the release (2 h ago), so the release is the leading suspect and rollback is the only candidate that addresses a cause rather than a symptom. Failover (b2) and read-replica routing (b5) relocate or offload load but carry a bad build with them; added capacity (b3) is a pre-peak measure that cannot be provisioned usefully mid-incident; circuit breakers (b4) fit partner-dependency failures, and nothing here points to an external dependency. I spend the single verification on memory_b1 because it is the load-bearing memory for my chosen action, and its summary hides the details that decide safety: whether that day-18 rollback happened under heavy write load, and whether the build carried schema or data migrations. If b1's original record shows it was a low-traffic, migration-free rollback, then 'no customer impact' does not transfer to settlement peak, and a backward-incompatible migration could mean losing customer writes on reversal — the one outcome the objective forbids. I did not verify b6 because staged gating is corroborative rather than decisive. Scale is deliberately guarded: per b6, canary cohorts surfaced regressions within an hour, so I roll back one write-path cohort first, confirming p99 recovery on the rolled-back slice while the rest stays on the current build as a control. That yields causal evidence rather than a coincidence, and bounds blast radius at peak. Uncertainty stands: the release may be innocent and this could be organic load growth plus settlement peak, in which case the canary shows no divergence and I escalate to capacity or replica offload in the next window instead of widening a rollback that is not fixing anything. If b1's archived record reveals migrations, I hold the rollback and pivot to read-replica offload (b5) as the write-safe option.
